characters: Dede: a curious girl of about four with two small puffs of hair, a green dress and shiny red rain boots.
Mama: Dede’s mother, kind and tall, in a patterned wrapper and a white top.
The butterfly: a small yellow butterfly with black-edged wings.

narrationPlan.voice: Soft, wondering storyteller voice with playful splash sounds
narrationPlan.pace: Very slow, with sound words acted out (about 85 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Gentle raindrop xylophone fading to soft sunshine strings (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Rain, tin roofs and shared yards are common in many Ghanaian neighbourhoods; Dede is a traditional Ga/Dangme name for a first-born daughter.

teacherGuide.overview: A quiet nature story built on a real observation: puddles shrink. Follow it with a safe water-watching activity.
learningGoals: Notice that water on the ground can dry up.
Use words such as puddle, splash, small and smaller.
Make a prediction and talk about it.

subjectLinks.subject: Science / Our World
subjectLinks.link: Weather and water in everyday life

beforeReading: Ask: have you ever jumped in a puddle?
whileReading: Pause at page 6 and ask where the water might go.
afterReading: Pour a little water on a slab or board in the sun and check it every 15 minutes.
Draw the “puddle getting smaller” in three steps.
discussion: Why did Dede wave at the face in the water?
What did the butterfly want from the puddle?
reflection: What do you like to do when it rains?

support: Use the pictures and gestures for each sound word.
stretch: Predict which will dry first: a big puddle or a small one.

culturalNotes: Rain, tin roofs and shared yards are common in many Ghanaian neighbourhoods; Dede is a traditional Ga/Dangme name for a first-born daughter.
localiseThis: Change the doll, boots and roof to match local experience.

investigation.title: Where does the water go?
steps: Pour a small puddle on the tile outside in the shade and another in the sun.
Draw round each puddle with chalk.
Check every 15 minutes and draw round again.
investigation.whatToNotice: The sunny puddle gets smaller faster. Children will not need the word “evaporation” yet.
investigation.safetyNote: Use clean water only and keep children on dry, level ground away from roads and drains.

factCheck.claim: Puddles shrink because the sun warms the water and some of it goes into the air.
factCheck.explanation: This is a simplified description of evaporation; part of a puddle also soaks into the ground.
factCheck.reference: Standard primary science resources (verify with the class textbook)
factCheck.analogyNote: “Lifted up into the sky” is a child-friendly picture, not a literal description.

reviewerNotes: Confirm language of origin and meaning before it appears in teacher notes.
